title: Continuous Space-Time Video Super-Resolution with 3D Fourier Fields
one_liner: Represent video as waves spread over space and time, so you can upsample at any scale without the errors that come from trying to guess missing frames.
lead: Video files are blocky because cameras capture pictures at fixed moments and with limited detail. To make videos smoother and sharper, older methods try to freeze one frame at a time, then guess where the action moved to in the next frame. This guessing breaks easily. This paper instead treats the whole video as one continuous wave pattern across space and time, letting the system answer what the picture looks like at any moment and zoom level without any guessing.

paras: Today's cameras record video by snapping pictures at fixed times and at fixed pixel grids. To make a video sharper or smoother, you need to invent pixels the camera never took. Old methods do this by guessing: they look at one frame, guess where things moved, and paste that knowledge onto the next frame. This is called frame warping, and it is fragile — if the guess about motion is even a little wrong, the next frame looks wrong.

A beginner might try: take each frame, make it sharper separately, then run them back together. But this fails because sharpness added frame-by-frame is choppy — the sharpness does not match between frames, and the picture flickers.

Better attempts separate the job: one network makes each frame sharper, another fills in new frames in between. But this approach fails because the networks fight each other — sharpening one frame wants to keep edges crisp, while frame-filling wants to blur across time to bridge the gap smoothly. Opposite goals trained at once cause the solution to be mediocre at both. They also cannot predict what a brand new moment in time should look like without first inventing intermediate frames, because neither network ever learns how things actually move or change in the real video.

callout.html: You cannot make a video both sharp and smooth if you process time and space as separate problems, or if you guess where things moved.

steps.text: Feed the blocky input into a neural network encoder.
Encoder predicts sine wave coefficients for a 3D grid over space and time.
To upsample, ask the wave model for pixel values at new (x, y, time) positions.
Apply a blur filter mathematically while sampling, so there are no jagged artifacts.
Output is sharp, smooth, and upsampledto any scale.

paras: The paper switches from separate spatial and temporal networks to a single spatio-temporal Fourier Field — a representation that treats space and time as one unified 3D volume. Instead of guessing where things move, it predicts the wave coefficients that describe the whole video at once.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: local wave phase
hidden.name: phase shift and scale per location
paras: The Fourier Field encodes video as a sum of up-and-down oscillating waves at different speeds. At each point in the 3D space-time grid, the method learns a phase shift (how far ahead or behind each wave oscillates at that location) and a scale (how tall each wave is). These two numbers determine what color or brightness the video has at that spot.

The neural encoder estimates these phase shifts and scales by looking at the low-quality input across a large spatio-temporal window. This is the hidden work — the encoder is learning where motion happens and how to represent fine detail as wave behavior, all implicitly encoded in those phase shifts.

heat.caption: Brighter means stronger wave amplitude at that location; borders mark locations with big motion or sharp edges.

reads.html: Imagine drawing a heat map over the video, where each spot gets marked with a sine wave that oscillates at different speeds. The phase shift says when that wave peaks at that spot; the scale says how big the oscillation is. These two numbers capture both motion and detail.

The method predicts voxel grids of local phase shifts and weighting coefficients for 3D Fourier basis functions, conditioned on the low-resolution input. This parametrization is compact (only two values per grid cell) but expressive enough to reconstruct sharp, temporally coherent video.

paras: Old methods fail because they separate space and time, or because they guess motion. This method works because it treats space and time as one 3D volume and expresses it as a sum of waves. Here is the mechanical chain:

Chain 1: No broken motion guessing. Instead of estimating optical flow (guessing where pixels moved), the method directly learns phase shifts — implicit motion information baked into the wave structure. A sine wave that peaks at different times at neighboring spatial locations naturally encodes motion, without ever computing a direction-and-speed number explicitly.

Chain 2: Sampling at any resolution. A sine wave is defined for all real numbers, not just integers. To upsample by two times or four times, you just ask the wave formula for values at coordinates between the originals, like 1.5 or 2.3. No frame interpolation network needed.

Chain 3: Sharp plus smooth together. Fourier waves naturally capture both fine spatial detail (high-frequency sine waves) and smooth motion over time (phase shifts that vary slowly). They are not fighting each other; they are part of one model.

Chain 4: Anti-aliasing built in. When sampling at a new resolution, the method multiplies by a Gaussian blur curve (point spread function) before summing. This cancels high-frequency noise that would make the output sparkly or aliased, directly fixing an artifact that plagues other upsampling methods.

stages.s: Neural encoder predicts phase shifts and scales
Query sine waves at new (x, y, time) positions

math.h2: The equation: a sum of waves
math.words: Video is estimated as the sum of sine and cosine waves, each with its own frequency, phase shift at each location, and amplitude scale. At each point in space-time, multiply the wave by a Gaussian to kill high-frequency noise, then sample.
math.equation: V_out(x, y, t) = sum_k a_k(x, y) * sin(2*pi*f_k*x + phi_k(x,y)) * cos(2*pi*g_k*y + psi_k(x,y)) * cos(2*pi*h_k*t + theta_k(x,y)) * Gaussian(x,y,t)
symbols: the output color or brightness at position (x,y) and time t
the amplitude scale of wave k at location (x, y), predicted by encoder
the frequency (how fast the wave oscillates) in x, y, t directions for basis k
the phase shift (where in the cycle the wave starts) at this location
a smooth blur weight that kills high-frequency noise, ensures anti-aliasing

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we want the brightness at position (2.5, 3.2, 0.4) in a low-res video upsampled 2x.
Wave k=1 oscillates with frequency 1 in x: phase 0.5. At x=2.5, the sine part = sin(2*pi*1*2.5 + 0.5) = sin(5*pi + 0.5) ≈ sin(0.5) ≈ 0.48.
Wave k=1 oscillates with frequency 1 in y: phase at (2.5, 3.2) is 0.3. The cosine part = cos(2*pi*1*3.2 + 0.3) = cos(6.4*pi + 0.3) ≈ cos(0.3) ≈ 0.96.
Wave k=1 oscillates with frequency 0.5 in time: phase at this location is 0.1. The time cosine = cos(2*pi*0.5*0.4 + 0.1) = cos(0.4*pi + 0.1) ≈ cos(1.35) ≈ 0.21.
Sum all k waves, get final brightness ≈ 120 (on 0-255 scale). Because the Gaussian is baked in, no sparkle or aliasing artifacts appear.

math.note: The phase shifts and scales are learned by the encoder from the low-resolution input, letting the system automatically find which wave frequencies describe the video best.

bars.h2: How much better: sharpness and smoothness

charts.title: Old separate-path methods
charts.note: Methods that sharpen frames one at a time then add interpolation are choppy and slow.

charts.title: This paper (V3)
charts.note: Unified wave model is sharper, smoother, and twice as fast because no frame guessing or warping.

items.html: Fourier methods sometimes make halos around very sharp edges (a phenomenon called Gibbs ringing). The Gaussian anti-aliasing filter reduces this, but cannot eliminate it completely on ultra-sharp boundaries like text.

The encoder looks at a fixed window of past and future frames to predict phase shifts. If an object moves faster than expected or farther than the encoder's receptive field, the model has not seen that motion and may fail to extrapolate smoothly, because the wave pattern was learned only from the limited input window, so predictions beyond that range are unreliable.

When something moves and reveals a new part of the scene (a disocclusion), no single wave pattern can describe it across time. The method must learn to 'break' the wave smoothness there, which requires explicit supervision.
When trained on videos with diverse motion, lighting, and scene changes, the model learns to adjust phase shifts adaptively and produces video that is both sharp and smooth across all scales.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A runnable demo should take a low-resolution video clip (say, 240 pixels wide at 30 frames per second), feed it through the trained model, and produce a high-resolution version (1920 pixels wide, or 120 frames per second). The output should show two things at once: (1) frame-by-frame close-ups showing that edges are sharp and textures are crisp, not blurry, and (2) a fast-motion scene (a ball rolling, a person walking) that looks smooth when played back, without jitter or ghosting.
demo.metric_eq: sharpness loss = sum of differences between upsampled frames and ground truth; smoothness = temporal consistency score (how similar neighboring frames look when aligned); speedup = time to upsample 100 frames at 4x spatial scale.
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss: a single unified Fourier model produces video that is sharp, smooth, and computed fast, without ever guessing motion or interpolating frames.
